title: The Clean Protocol
premise: Lior Halloran, a financial-crimes investigator who has spent seven years untangling laundered money for a compliance firm that keeps rewriting its own rules, receives a debt notice from a stranger named Marek Voss claiming she once saved his life — a favor she has no memory of. The 'interest' he demands is her help moving a sum through channels only she can read, and when she traces it, she uncovers a plot to destroy a border checkpoint during a shift change, timed to look like a gas-main accident. As Lior races to decode the money's final destination, she discovers the favor was real: as a child, displaced and nameless, she was smuggled across that same border by Voss, and her entire identity was built on documents he forged. In the end, Lior exposes the attack to authorities she no longer trusts, chooses to testify about her own fabricated past at the cost of her career, and stops the bombing minutes before the shift change — inheriting not money, but the truth of who she is.
about_author: Lena Sandoval is a former anti-money-laundering analyst who left banking after a decade of watching clean money do dirty work. She writes thrillers from a small coastal town, drawing on case files she probably shouldn't have memorized.

chapters.title: Interest Owed
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. A certified letter arrives from Marek Voss thanking her for a favor from 1994 — one she never performed — with a demand for repayment in kind. She dismisses it as fraud, but the letter contains a detail about her childhood no stranger could know. Emotional beat: unease beneath routine.

chapters.title: Clean Money, Dirty Hands
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. At Halvern Compliance, Lior flags an unusual pattern of shell transfers routed toward a border logistics company. Her supervisor buries the report under new 'materiality thresholds.' She pockets a copy. Beat: professional pride curdling into suspicion.

chapters.title: The Stranger at the Laundromat
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Voss watches Lior from across the street, rehearsing what he'll say. Flashback fragments reveal he tracked her for months before sending the letter. He knows the deadline better than she does. Beat: tenderness tangled with menace.

chapters.title: Thresholds
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior follows the shell-company thread to a warehouse lease signed by a man who died two years ago. Someone is resurrecting dead signatures — including, she realizes with a chill, possibly her father's. Beat: the ground tilting.

chapters.title: A Favor That Never Happened
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Lior confronts Voss; he tells her she saved him crossing the border as children, and shows her a photograph of two kids she doesn't recognize — one wearing her face. Beat: vertigo of a memory that isn't hers but fits perfectly.

chapters.title: The Halloran File
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior pulls her own adoption records and finds gaps: no hospital record, a birth certificate issued eleven months late, a sponsoring priest with ties to the same logistics company. Beat: identity cracking open like ice.

chapters.title: Shift Change
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Voss meets the plotters he's infiltrated — men planning to destroy the Kestrel Crossing checkpoint during the 6 a.m. shift change, disguised as a gas-main failure. He needs Lior to trace their funding because he can't get close enough. Beat: dread with a countdown attached.

chapters.title: Materiality
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior reports the anomaly internally and is offered a promotion contingent on dropping it. Her mentor, Ruth, quietly warns her that the last analyst who pushed died in a car accident. Beat: temptation versus conscience.

chapters.title: What the Money Remembers
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Following the funds backward, Lior reconstructs a smuggling network from twenty years ago — the same one that carried her across. Every account is a fossil of someone's desperation, maybe her parents'. Beat: grief surfacing through spreadsheets.

chapters.title: The Priest's Ledger
chapters.summary: Lior and Voss POV. They find the dead priest's hidden ledger in a chapel basement: names of smuggled children, payments, and a page torn out — the page with Lior's original name. Beat: hope sharpened into obsession.

chapters.title: Ruth's Warning
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth reveals she helped bury the earlier investigation to protect her family, and begs Lior to walk away. Lior refuses. Their friendship fractures. Beat: betrayal as an act of love.

chapters.title: Dead Signature
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The man whose signature opened the warehouse lease turns out to be alive, hiding, and terrified — he confirms the attack plan and gives her a burner number before disappearing. Beat: first hard proof, first real danger.

chapters.title: Tail Lights
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior realizes she's being followed and runs a counter-surveillance route through the old market district where she grew up. Voss extracts her, and they argue about whether to go to police who may be compromised. Beat: fear becoming resolve.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Voss confesses he kept the torn ledger page for twenty years: Lior's birth name, her mother's handwriting. He withheld it to guarantee her help, and now must admit the manipulation. Beat: trust nearly destroyed, then rebuilt on honesty.

chapters.title: Follow the Money Down
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Working through the night, Lior maps the full funding chain to its terminus: a demolition contractor paid through the border authority itself. The attack isn't just planned — it's insured. Beat: horror at how clean it all looks.

chapters.title: Complicity
chapters.summary: Supervisor Dane's POV. Dane learns Lior has the map and makes calls upstairs. We see the machinery of cover-up from inside: bonuses, threats, a quiet history of bought silence. Beat: banality of evil.

chapters.title: Seventy-Two Hours
chapters.summary: Lior and Voss POV. With three days until the shift change, Lior takes the evidence to a federal contact who hesitates — jurisdictional turf, an election year. She decides to prepare a parallel track: the press, and the checkpoint workers themselves. Beat: agency seized.

chapters.title: The Whistle Before the Train
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior briefs the checkpoint union steward anonymously while Voss feeds the contractor false scheduling data to buy time. Dane suspends Lior, confiscating her credentials. Beat: sacrifice made concrete.

chapters.title: Kestrel Crossing
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs, short sections. Dawn at the checkpoint. The gas crew arrives early. Lior, locked out of official channels, drives to the crossing herself with the evidence and a phone line open to a journalist. Beat: breathless acceleration.

chapters.title: Six O'Clock
chapters.summary: Climax. Lior blocks the access road as the detonator timer runs; Voss confronts the bomber inside the pump house. The journalist's broadcast forces federal agents to move. The explosion fails; the bomber is taken; Voss is wounded shielding a worker. Beat: everything staked, everything risked.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. In a hearing room, Lior testifies not only about the plot but about her forged identity, surrendering her clearance and her name. Ruth corroborates at cost to herself. Beat: grief and liberation braided together.

chapters.title: The Name She Keeps
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Lior's POV. Months later, Lior visits the restored checkpoint, then the chapel where the ledger rests in an archive. She signs a document — her new legal name, chosen freely — and mails Voss, recovering in the north, a letter that begins: 'Consider the debt paid.' Beat: belonging, finally self-made.
